content:
The former Liberal minister Philip Ruddock has been appointed by the Australian cabinet to review whether the country’s laws sufficiently protect the human right to religious freedom. This move, announced on Wednesday, aims to preempt a contentious debate about religious exemptions in the context of the same-sex marriage bill.

***

Treasurer Scott Morrison clarified that Ruddock’s review is not a replacement for the religious amendments being considered in the marriage equality legislation. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull emphasized the need for a careful examination of religious freedom, especially following the successful "yes" vote for same-sex marriage and the impending legislation on the issue.

***

There is division within the government on the timing of addressing religious freedom. Some conservatives, like Peter Dutton and Mathias Cormann, suggest a separate religious freedom bill could be considered next year, while others, including Morrison and Senator David Fawcett, argue it should be tackled alongside the marriage bill. Ruddock has been given a deadline of March 31 to complete his report.

***

Turnbull cautioned that many proposed legislative changes to protect religious freedom extend beyond the immediate marriage equality debate. He warned of the risks of unintended consequences when parliament attempts to legislate protections for fundamental rights like religious freedom, particularly if broad, rights-style declarations are used.

***
The prime minister justified Ruddock’s appointment, citing his experience as Australia’s special envoy for human rights. Turnbull described the review as a timely "expert stocktake" to guide any potential legislative reforms on religious freedom.
